title: All-Island Resource Adequacy Assessment 2025-2034
authors: EirGrid (analysis team; no named authors on the pages read)
institution: EirGrid (Ireland's transmission system operator), with SONI and supported by CRU
verification: EirGrid announcement/summary page read at origin 2026-11-05; full AIRAA document not read.
relevance: EirGrid's successor to the Generation Capacity Statement, the official 10-year supply-demand outlook for Ireland - the European country most associated with data-centre grid strain. It projects median-scenario electricity demand up 45% between 2023 and 2034, peak demand up 24% (past 7,000 MW by 2034, after a record 6,024 MW peak on 8 January 2025), and flags a 600-800 MW adequacy gap in challenging conditions for 2028-2032 plus 100-1,000 MW more capacity needed in 2032-2034. The methodology was aligned to the European (ENTSO-E) resource-adequacy framework, and the authors note the demand data freeze (30 April 2024) predates the 2025 Programme for Government. The summary page does not break out the data-centre share of demand (earlier EirGrid statements put it around a fifth to a quarter of demand by 2030), so the DC-specific numbers must be taken from companion publications.

title: Capaciteitskaart (national grid capacity map) - waar is er nog ruimte op het elektriciteitsnet
authors: Netbeheer Nederland (association of Dutch electricity and gas grid operators)
institution: Netbeheer Nederland
verification: Official informational landing page read at origin 2026-11-05 (interactive map at capaciteitskaart.netbeheernederland.nl not machine-readable); launch date and update cadence not stated on the page read.
relevance: The Dutch grid operators' official, regularly updated map showing per-region where transport capacity for large connections (consumption and feed-in) is available, constrained or unavailable - the instrument a data-centre developer in the Netherlands must consult before applying for a connection, and one the IEA cited in its March 2025 commentary on grid congestion. It exists because fast-growing demand has produced queues of large consumers who cannot connect simultaneously in parts of the country; secondary Dutch sources describe roughly 12,000 parties waiting for consumption connections and congestion costing an estimated EUR 40 billion a year (attributed to sector estimates, not this page). The page read is qualitative - it does not publish MW figures or congestion percentages, which sit in the map application and underlying operator datasets.

title: The 11th Basic Plan for Supply and Demand of Power (2024-2038), confirmed 21 February 2025
authors: Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy (MOTIE), Republic of Korea
institution: Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy (MOTIE), Republic of Korea
access: open page (official plan in Korean; English summaries by law firms and analysts)
verification: Lead: MOTIE's Korean original not directly readable; the Shin & Kim newsletter (13 March 2025) summarizing the plan's energy-mix tables was read in full on 2026-11-05, with analyst (IEEFA, IRC) corroboration via search results.
relevance: Korea's definitive 15-year electricity plan, finalized amid political turmoil and explicitly updated for semiconductor and data-centre demand growth, which independent analyses (IRC Consulting Korea) say drives roughly 1.8% average annual demand growth through 2038. The confirmed plan puts generation at 642.6 TWh in 2030 and 704.5 TWh in 2038, with nuclear rising to 35.2% (248.3 TWh), renewables to 33.0% (232.1 TWh), and zero-carbon sources to 70.7% by 2038; it adds two new nuclear plants plus one domestic SMR and early BESS deployment in Honam. For the AI-infrastructure story it shows how a top-5 semiconductor economy is re-planning its grid around large-load growth, including PPA market reforms and low-interest loans that hyperscalers and data-centre operators would use. Limitations: the sources read do not state the data-centre-specific demand line (that sits in the Korean annexes), and the plan must be revised every two years, so figures may shift in the imminent 12th plan.

title: 2050年度までの全国の長期電力需要想定 報告書 (Long-term national electricity demand outlook to FY2050)
authors: OCCTO (Organization for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators), based on CRIEPI long-term demand assumptions
institution: OCCTO (Japan's cross-regional transmission coordinator)
verification: Metadata only (lead): the 86-page PDF could not be parsed via WebFetch on 2026-11-05; figures read come from WebSearch result summaries of the OCCTO report and the related METI advisory document and CRIEPI study (serc25001).
relevance: Japan's official grid-coordination outlook that, for the first time, explicitly models data-centre and semiconductor-fab demand out to 2050: it projects total national demand could reach a maximum of about 1,250 TWh by FY2050, roughly 45% above FY2024 actuals, driven by AI and data centres. Its scenario work shows peak demand from new data centres and fabs rising from +0.56 GW in FY2025 to +7.15 GW by FY2034, and commentary on the report warns that even with thermal replacement, supply capacity may fall short in the highest-demand scenario. This is the primary quantitative anchor for the Japan grid angle of the AI buildout, complementing IEEJ's economic outlook. Limitations: scenario-based and sensitive to assumptions, and only search-level summaries could be read; the report itself is Japanese-language.

title: Philippine Energy Plan 2023-2050
authors: Department of Energy (DOE), Republic of the Philippines
institution: Department of Energy (DOE), Republic of the Philippines
access: open PDF (official volumes on doe.gov.ph; summary via Climate Change Laws of the World)
verification: Lead: the doe.gov.ph PEP page returned a Page Not Found error on 2026-11-05; the Climate Change Laws of the World catalogue page (Grantham Institute summary) was read at origin, and World Bank and IMF summaries of the plan's demand projections were read via search results.
relevance: The Philippines' flagship national energy plan, relevant to Southeast Asia's fastest-growing electricity markets where the government is courting data-centre and semiconductor investment. It targets over 40% renewable energy in the total energy mix by 2030 and surpassing 50% by 2040, incorporates a first nuclear-power pathway, and - per the World Bank's October 2024 reading - projects Philippine electricity demand to more than quadruple between 2023 and 2050. It bundles instruments (green energy auctions that awarded 21 GW of solar against a 10 GW target per MBC's July 2024 note, zoning, direct investment) that shape whether AI-era load can be served cleanly. Limitations: the catalogue summary read does not mention data centres explicitly, and demand-side detail requires the full Volumes I-III.

title: Decision No. 768/QD-TTg approving the adjustment of the National Power Development Plan VIII (PDP8) for 2021-2030, vision to 2050
authors: Prime Minister Pham Minh Chinh, Government of Vietnam
institution: Office of the Government of Vietnam (official English translation hosted by the Vietnam Energy Partnership Group)
verification: Lead: the official English translation PDF could not be parsed via WebFetch on 2026-11-05; the US International Trade Administration summary (dated 22 August 2025) was read in full, with KPMG and law-firm summaries of the Decision read via search results.
relevance: The revised PDP8 is Vietnam's binding plan for powering one of Asia's fastest-growing manufacturing and data-centre destinations, issued four months before the country's Digital Technology Industry Law (already catalogued) made AI data centres eligible for special investment incentives. It raises 2030 targets to 26,066-38,029 MW of onshore/nearshore wind (from 21,880 MW), 17,032 MW of offshore wind (from 6,000 MW) and 10,000-16,300 MW of battery storage (from 300 MW), brings nuclear back with Ninh Thuan 1 and 2 at 4,000-6,400 MW expected 2030-2035, and prices the plan at USD 134.7 billion to 2030 and up to USD 523 billion to 2050 (all figures from the ITA summary). Analysts note roughly 25% of system capacity is expected to be reachable via direct power purchase agreements, the mechanism large consumers such as data centres would use to contract renewables. Limitations: the sources read give no explicit data-centre demand line; that discussion sits in Vietnamese planning annexes.

title: Thailand Board of Investment approves seven new data centre and data hosting projects (first board meeting of 2026)
authors: Thailand Board of Investment (BOI)
institution: Thailand Board of Investment (BOI), Office of the Prime Minister
verification: Lead: the official boi.go.th press-release page rendered empty via WebFetch on 2026-11-05; the same figures and company list were read in full from The Story Thailand's coverage of the 16 January 2026 board meeting, and the official 2025 cumulative total (36 projects, THB 728 billion) was corroborated across multiple search results citing the BOI release.
relevance: The official Thai investment-promotion record of the country's data-centre surge: at its January 2026 board meeting the BOI approved seven projects worth over USD 3.1 billion (THB 96.88 billion) from True Internet Data Center (3 projects, ~223 MW, ~USD 1.4 billion), GSA Data Center 05 (~120 MW), Stellar DC (25 MW, with SENA/SC Zeus) and Freyr Technology, across Bangkok, Chonburi, Rayong, Samut Prakan and the Eastern Economic Corridor. It follows a 2025 pipeline of 36 data-centre projects worth over THB 728 billion (~USD 23.1 billion) and BOI incentives including uncapped 8-year corporate income tax exemptions for qualifying data-centre and cloud projects. This is the primary administrative source for how a Southeast Asian state is underwriting AI-adjacent construction with fiscal incentives. Limitations: approvals are announced capacity, not energized load, and no electricity or water sourcing data is given.

title: Komdigi fokus selesaikan standar pusat data berkelanjutan Indonesia (Komdigi focuses on completing Indonesia's sustainable data centre standard)
authors: Kementerian Komunikasi dan Digital (Komdigi), Directorate General of Digital Infrastructure (DJID); reporting by DJID newsroom
institution: Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs (Komdigi), Republic of Indonesia
verification: Full article read at origin 2026-11-05.
relevance: The Indonesian digital-ministry record of a national sustainable-data-centre standard under development, worked out with the industry association IDPRO, PLN, other ministries, universities and tech companies at an 28 August 2025 forum. A ministry strategy official (Denny Setiawan) states the standard is meant as shared reference rather than new red tape, covering electrical systems, connectivity, uptime, energy efficiency and environmental sustainability, and projects the data-centre industry to grow tenfold within five years. Notably for the geography of the buildout, the ministry urges development beyond Jakarta and Batam - toward Surabaya, Kupang and even Jayapura - with faster permitting, positioning Indonesia's response to Vietnam and Thailand. Limitations: it is a ministry news post, so it names no draft clauses, PUE thresholds or enforcement mechanisms, which will only appear when the standard is finalized.

title: Taiwan's Data Centers Still Use Less Than 1% of the Island's Electricity. So Why Is the Grid Already Under Strain?
authors: Huang Hao-Min, Sun Wen-Lin (The Reporter), with data analysis by Chien Yi-Hui and Fang Te-Lin; cross-border investigation with the Environmental Reporting Collective
institution: The Reporter (報導者), Taiwan's nonprofit investigative newsroom
verification: Full English-language article read at origin 2026-11-05.
relevance: A data-driven Taiwanese investigation that reconstructs, from Taipower records and interviews with Google, Chunghwa, Chief Telecom, Delta, ITRI and officials, how AI data centres interact with a constrained grid: as of November 2025 Taipower had received 79 AI data-centre power applications totalling about 4,758 MW, approved 40 (~3,033 MW) and rejected 39, yet over 70% of approved capacity lapsed after applicants missed the six-month initiation window, and only about 870.5 MW (four sites drawing ~303.5 MW plus five under construction) is real. Data centres use under 1% of Taiwan's ~282.8 billion kWh (sales category up from ~730 million kWh in 2021 to ~1.5 billion in 2025), while semiconductors took 42.38 billion kWh - nearly 15% - and Taipower projects semiconductors plus AI industries will add over 5 GW by 2030. Since 2024 Taipower has suspended new connections above 5 MW north of Taoyuan, and in November 2025 the MOEA brought >5 MW data centres under energy-use review with PUE thresholds (below 1.3 hyperscale, 1.4 colocation). Limitations acknowledged by the authors: Taipower does not disclose per-site loads, so site figures are estimates and its 1.85 GW AI forecast is contested by interviewees.

title: Federal Government unveils National Digital Cloud Policy to drive investment, digital sovereignty and government transformation
authors: Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy (FMCIDE), under Minister Dr. 'Bosun Tijani
institution: Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy (FMCIDE), Nigeria; oversight by NITDA, delivery by Galaxy Backbone
verification: Full announcement read at origin 2026-11-05; companion NITDA documents (National Cloud Investment Strategy 2025, National Guideline for Cloud Computing 2026) identified via search but the PDFs could not be parsed.
relevance: Nigeria's official cloud-and-data-centre policy, superseding the 2019 Cloud Computing Policy, that quantifies the investment pull the government is attempting: US$250 million of private investment within 12 months rising to US$750 million within 24 months, plus targets for compliant hosting capacity, regional capacity contracted from Nigeria, and digital-service exports aimed at making Nigeria a hosting hub for West Africa. It pairs a Cloud-First mandate for federal agencies with deliberately narrow sovereignty rules (presidential approval only for designated sovereign data) and offers fiscal and regulatory incentives for data-centre investment, explicitly including support addressing Nigeria's energy constraints. The 24-month roadmap ties in Project BRIDGE (90,000 km of fibre) and the 3MTT skills programme, showing how connectivity and compute supply chains are being planned together. Limitations: it is a policy announcement - no baseline data-centre capacity or power figures are given, and delivery depends on the NITDA implementing documents not read here.

title: Konza Cloud Expansion and Smart City Facilities - Feasibility Study Report, Executive Summary (Annex I to Addendum II)
authors: Konza Technopolis Development Authority (KoTDA) with PPP transaction advisors
institution: Konza Technopolis Development Authority (KoTDA), Government of Kenya
verification: Metadata only (lead): the 21-page executive-summary PDF could not be parsed via WebFetch on 2026-11-05; its scope was established through search-result summaries, the Konza Technopolis landing page read at origin, and PPP Kenya transaction-advisory documents.
relevance: Kenya's state flagship for sovereign cloud and data-centre capacity: the feasibility study underpins a public-private partnership to expand the Tier III (Uptime Institute-certified) Konza National Data Centre and its Konza Sovereign Cloud, explicitly integrating environmental sustainability as a feasibility criterion and supporting the Kenya AI Strategy 2025-2030. Konza's cloud platform already hosts 145 of Kenya's 451 government systems/services according to a 2026 data-maturity assessment, and the project was admitted into Kenya's PPP pipeline in December 2025 with National Treasury transaction advisory support, framed as safeguarding national data under data-protection law. It is a concrete Global South example of a state building compute infrastructure as an industrial-policy asset rather than leaving it to hyperscalers. Limitations: the executive summary's financial, MW and storage figures could not be read directly, so the record relies on catalogue-level descriptions.

title: La huella que dejan las nubes (The footprint the clouds leave behind)
authors: Paola Ricaurte, Lorena Rios, Aurora Gomez Delgado (field research); Oxfam Mexico and Oxfam Intermón
institution: Oxfam Mexico / Oxfam Intermón
verification: Full bulletin (in Spanish) read at origin 2026-11-05.
relevance: A field investigation of the Queretaro data-centre cluster - which concentrates roughly half of Mexico's data-centre energy capacity - pairing interviews in Colon and El Marques with analysis of permits: more than 90% of Queretaro's territory was in drought in 2024 and 2025, one Microsoft campus holds well permits of up to 25 million litres of groundwater a year, and a single large data centre can consume up to 19 million litres a day (a city of 50,000). It documents CloudHQ's projected six facilities at 190.26 MW initially with a future load of 900 MW (equivalent to 2.6 million homes' consumption by its arithmetic), and contrasts inflated job promises (AWS 7,000, Google 117,000, Microsoft ~300,000 cited in discourse) with the ~200 permanent jobs a typical data centre runs. The authors call for binding regulation: transparency, resource-consumption limits, rigorous environmental review and tax frameworks that avoid socializing costs. Limitations: industrial water and energy figures rest on permits and company disclosures that are themselves incomplete because data centres are classified as service enterprises and often lack public environmental impact assessments.

title: World's first tropical climate data centre testbed opens (Singapore Tropical Data Centre Testbed, STDCT)
authors: Programme Director Assoc. Prof. Lee Poh Seng (NUS); Co-Director Prof. Wen Yonggang (NTU); NUS College of Design and Engineering newsroom
institution: National University of Singapore and Nanyang Technological University, funded by the National Research Foundation (RIE2025) with IMDA support
verification: Full NUS news release read at origin 2026-11-05.
relevance: The primary announcement of the world's first tropical-climate data-centre testbed, a full-scale 770 m2 live facility at NUS jointly led by NUS and NTU with more than S$30 million of investment across five research projects and 20 industry collaborators. It targets cuts of up to 40% in energy, 30-40% in water use and ~40% in CO2 (to under 0.54 million tons/year) and a PUE below 1.2 - against Singapore's 1.3 regulatory requirement and a stated 2022 global average of 1.5 - by testing immersion and direct-chip hybrid cooling, hygroscopic-material cooling, optimized tropical air-cooling setpoints and an AI-driven digital twin. For the engineering side of the water/cooling story it is the reference experiment showing how hot-humid countries can operate dense AI compute efficiently. Limitations: the release states targets for mid-2024 rather than final measured results, which appear in later project publications.

title: Green Data Centre Roadmap: Charting green growth for data centres in Singapore
authors: Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), with the Economic Development Board for the DC-CFA schemes
institution: Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), Singapore
access: open page (roadmap PDF open; factsheet referenced)
verification: Lead: the IMDA page read at origin 2026-11-05 rendered only navigation; substantive contents (300 MW target, PUE/green-energy criteria, DC-CFA2) were read in full from the Norton Rose Fulbright analysis of the Roadmap and DC-CFA2, and the 30 May 2024 ATxSummit launch date was confirmed across multiple search sources.
relevance: Singapore's flagship policy for reconciling its AI ambitions with land and power scarcity, launched 30 May 2024: it commits to at least 300 MW of new data-centre capacity in the near term, with more released in cycles tied to green-energy adoption, and aims for energy-efficient compute across all Singapore data centres within a decade. Its successor call for applications (DC-CFA2, launched 1 December 2025) allocates at least 200 MW and requires PUE of at most 1.25 at full IT load, BCA-IMDA Green Mark Platinum certification, IT efficiency to SS 715:2025, and at least 50% green energy via pathways such as biomethane, low-carbon hydrogen or fuel cells with CCS, with a WUE benchmark of at most 2.0 cubic metres per MWh. It is the clearest national example of using capacity rations and sustainability criteria to steer which AI compute gets built where. Limitations: the criteria summaries read are secondary legal analyses; compliance outcomes will only show in future allocations, and the hot-humid climate makes ultra-low PUE costly.

title: The Intersection of Data Center Development, Water Availability, and Environmental Justice in California
authors: Iris Stewart-Frey and Irina Raicu (Santa Clara University), research for Next 10
institution: Next 10 (nonpartisan nonprofit) with Santa Clara University researchers
verification: Publication page read at origin 2026-11-05; full PDF not read.
relevance: Described by Next 10 as the first comprehensive analysis of every known operating and planned California data centre through a combined water-access and environmental-justice lens: the Santa Clara University team built a statewide facility database and new GIS indices of water scarcity and community vulnerability, with five case studies (Sacramento, Los Angeles, Santa Clara; planned facilities in Imperial County and Gilroy). It finds that for most facilities there are no publicly accessible environmental planning documents and no data on cooling systems or water source; that water-scarcity risk is highest in the Central and Imperial Valleys where at least two massive new projects are planned; and that newer hyperscale sites are increasingly located in socially and hydrologically vulnerable regions unlike the earlier urban tech-hub pattern, while groundwater-dependent towns like Gilroy face outsized drought risk. Recommendations include disclosure laws with audits, recycled-water incentives, and greater water-provider engagement. Limitations stated by the authors: the lack of public water-use and cooling data that motivates the report also constrains it.

title: Life-Cycle Emissions of AI Hardware: A Cradle-To-Grave Approach and Generational Trends
authors: Ian Schneider, Hui Xu, Stephan Benecke, David Patterson, Keguo Huang, Parthasarathy Ranganathan, Cooper Elsworth
institution: Google (arXiv preprint; later published in IEEE Multimedia)
verification: Abstract and metadata read at origin (arXiv) 2026-11-05; full PDF not read.
relevance: The first published comprehensive life-cycle assessment of AI accelerator hardware: the Google team conducted a cradle-to-grave greenhouse-gas LCA across five generations of its TPU accelerators, covering raw-material extraction, manufacturing, disposal and operational energy during development, deployment and model serving, using first-party data. It publishes the first manufacturing-emissions figures for an AI accelerator and introduces compute carbon intensity (CCI), a metric for comparing hardware sustainability and estimating training/inference footprints; CCI improves about 3x from TPU v4i to TPU v6e, with software gains amplifying hardware improvements. This is the key peer-visible source showing embodied emissions are a material share of AI's footprint, complementing the Greenpeace chip-manufacturing study already catalogued. Limitations stated on the abstract page: it covers only Google TPUs and rests on single-company first-party data, so vendor generality and independent verification are limited; per-chip tCO2e values require the full text.

title: E-waste challenges of generative artificial intelligence
authors: Peng Wang, Ling-Yu Zhang (Key Lab of Urban Environment and Health, Institute of Urban Environment, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Xiamen), Asaf Tzachor (Reichman University, Israel; University of Cambridge), Wei-Qiang Chen (CAS IUE)
institution: Chinese Academy of Sciences Institute of Urban Environment, with Reichman University and University of Cambridge (Nature Computational Science, vol. 4, pp. 818-823)
access: open page (abstract and framing open; full text paywalled)
verification: Article page (abstract-level) read at origin 2026-11-05 after redirect handling; full text and figure details paywalled.
relevance: The first study to quantify the e-waste footprint of generative AI: the authors build a computational-power-driven material flow analysis linking LLM computing-power growth to server and chip demand, projecting 1.2-5.0 million tons of cumulative LLM-related e-waste during 2020-2030 absent mitigation. They quantify that circular-economy strategies across the generative-AI value chain (component reuse, chip recycling, lifetime extension) could cut e-waste generation by 16-86%, and warn that semiconductor import restrictions and rapid server turnover for cost savings could intensify the waste stream. Code and scenario data are openly available on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.13790035). Limitations stated by the authors: results are highly sensitive to uncertain AI growth rates, server lifetimes and geopolitics, hence the wide range; the 2023 baseline and strategy-by-strategy breakdown sit in the paywalled text.

title: Data Centre Energy Use: Critical Review of Models and Results
authors: George Kamiya, Vlad C. Coroama
institution: EDNA - Energy Efficient End-use Equipment Technology Collaboration Programme (4E TCP), International Energy Agency family
access: open page (full report via registration/download link)
verification: Publication page read at origin 2026-11-05 (72-page PDF not read); authorship and page count confirmed via the IEA 4E publication listing in search results.
relevance: The most systematic audit of why data-centre energy estimates disagree: the authors reviewed more than 100 articles, reports and statistical sources published since 2014, spanning thousands of estimates and projections for 2010-2040 across over 200 scenarios, and find estimates for 2020 ranging from under 200 TWh to 1,200 TWh and 2030 projections from just over 200 TWh to nearly 8,000 TWh - a spread of nearly a factor of 40 that confuses policymakers. The report establishes a plausible current range and distils best practices and pitfalls for future assessments, making it the methodological referee for every headline number (including IEA's ~415 TWh) used in the AI-energy debate. It also covers African capacity context (most of the continent's ~300 MW in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria per search-result excerpts). Limitations: it reviews rather than produces primary measurements, and the headline range depends on how one weights bottom-up versus top-down methods.

title: Preliminary Analysis of Nuclear-Powered Data Center Scenarios
authors: Idaho National Laboratory Systems Analysis and Integration team (authors listed in the OSTI record, bibliographic ID 3001074)
institution: Idaho National Laboratory (INL), managed by Battelle Energy Alliance for the US Department of Energy Office of Nuclear Energy
verification: Report landing page (abstract-level) read at origin 2026-11-05; full OSTI-hosted report not read.
relevance: A US national-lab systems analysis of coupling nuclear plants - including small modular reactors - to data centres, examining optimal reactor sizing and deployment scenarios, urban versus rural siting feasibility, and local economic and socio-environmental impacts, as the technical companion to DOE's September 2025 call for proposals to build AI data centres powered by nuclear projects on the INL site. It sits alongside INL's broader data-centre programme (funded by DOE's Office of Electricity), which notes data centres are expected to drive about 20% of US energy demand growth by 2030 and offers no-cost technical assistance on SMR integration readiness, flexible interconnection and secure digital substations. For the nuclear/clean-firm sub-area it is the primary engineering-economics source from the laboratory actually running the experiments. Limitations: the landing page gives no headline GW or cost numbers (these are in the OSTI full text) and the analysis is explicitly preliminary, recommending further study.

title: Data center waste heat for district heating networks: A review
authors: Xiaolei Yuan, Jiayi Liu, Sijia Sun, Xiaojie Lin, Xiaojun Fan, Weixin Zhao, Risto Kosonen
institution: Aalto University (Finland) and collaborators (Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, vol. 219, article 115863)
verification: Lead: ScienceDirect blocked WebFetch (auth redirect) on 2026-11-05; bibliographic metadata confirmed via Crossref API (authors, RSER vol. 219, 115863, September 2025), and the abstract's opening scope was read via search-index excerpts and the Aalto research portal listing.
relevance: The most-cited recent peer-reviewed review of integrating data-centre waste heat into district heating networks, evaluating technical, energy, economic and environmental potential - the academic reference for the heat-reuse sub-area. The co-author team is anchored at Aalto University, where Risto Kosonen leads HVAC and data-centre energy-efficiency research, and the review has accumulated on the order of 110 citations within about a year per Google Scholar indexing. It frames which temperature levels, heat-pump upgrades and network distances make reuse viable, complementing sector estimates that 997 EU-28 data centres sit within 2 km of a district-heating network representing more than 75 TWh/year of accessible excess heat (an EUDCA/ICEF figure). Limitations: it synthesizes published cases rather than measuring new sites, and the paywalled text was not read, so country-by-country numbers cannot be quoted from the full article.

title: ITU DataHub - free access to the World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators data
authors: ITU ICT Data and Analytics Division (Telecommunication Development Bureau)
institution: International Telecommunication Union (ITU), United Nations agency
verification: ITU's World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators Database page read at origin 2026-11-05 (stating the paid database was discontinued in 2024 and all data is now free on the DataHub); the datahub.itu.int portal itself returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, and coverage figures (200+ economies, 100+ indicators) come from ITU publication pages via search results.
relevance: The official free successor to the paid World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators Database: in 2024 ITU discontinued the subscription product and moved all of its collected data to the DataHub, making per-country broadband penetration, fixed/mobile subscriptions, prices, traffic and coverage indicators freely downloadable - the authoritative public-input layer for assessing which countries can plausibly host AI-relevant digital infrastructure. ITU publication pages describe data for over 200 economies, and the dataset is mirrored in the World Bank's Data360 platform (ITU_DH) for programmatic use. For the connectivity sub-area it is the free alternative to commercial trackers like TeleGeography for national ICT indicators. Limitations: it measures connectivity and affordability, not cable-level or data-centre capacity, and the Terms of Use apply; the portal blocked automated access during verification.

title: African Undersea Cables - a free, community-updated map and ownership matrix of Africa's submarine fibre systems
authors: Steve Song (independent researcher; former Shuttleworth Foundation telecommunication fellow)
institution: Many Possibilities (independent research project, Version 57, update September 2025)
verification: Map page read at origin 2026-11-05 (Version 57, September 2025 update; 463-reader comment thread).
relevance: The open, two-decade alternative to commercial cable maps for Africa: Song's map and investor/ownership matrix cover the continent's submarine systems from SAT-3/SAFE and SEACOM through EASSy, WACS, ACE, SAIL, PEACE and 2Africa/Equiano, with per-cable ownership shares and ready-for-service dates, maintained through an open community-corrections process (463 comments feeding revisions) and offered in SVG on request. It is widely cited in academic and policy work on African connectivity because it shows not just where cables land but who owns them - a governance question for AI-era data-centre siting in Lagos, Mombasa or Cape Town. Song explicitly curates (excluding some Mediterranean systems) and links out to TeleGeography for global coverage, positioning the map as the free Africa-focused complement. Limitations: it is a one-maintainer curated artefact rather than an authoritative registry, and capacity pricing detail is answered informally rather than published systematically.
